content: Sucralfate can reduce the absorption and effectiveness of digoxin when both are taken orally, due to inhibition of gastrointestinal absorption. It is recommended to avoid this combination or use an alternative drug. The digoxin dose may need to be increased by approximately 20% to 40%. Sucralfate also decreases the absorption and effectiveness of dolutegravir by binding to cations in the gastrointestinal tract. To minimize this interaction, dolutegravir should be taken either two hours before or six hours after sucralfate or other medications containing polyvalent cations. Similarly, sucralfate reduces the absorption of bictegravir through cation binding in the gastrointestinal tract. Bictegravir should be taken on an empty stomach at least two hours before or six hours after antacids containing aluminum, magnesium, or calcium. Routine simultaneous administration of bictegravir with these antacids is not recommended. The absorption of ciprofloxacin is significantly reduced when taken with sucralfate due to chelation in the gastrointestinal tract. To avoid this interaction, ciprofloxacin should be taken two hours before or six hours after sucralfate. Sucralfate decreases the absorption of delafloxacin by forming chelates with alkaline earth and transition metal cations. Delafloxacin should be administered at least two hours before or six hours after sucralfate. The absorption of other medications, such as fleroxacin, gemifloxacin, ketoconazole, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, ofloxacin, and tetracyclines (including doxycycline, minocycline, and oxytetracycline), is also reduced by sucralfate due to inhibition of gastrointestinal absorption. These drugs should be taken at least two hours before or six hours after sucralfate to minimize interactions. Sucralfate can reduce the effectiveness of furosemide by inhibiting its gastrointestinal absorption. When both drugs are used together, the natriuretic and antihypertensive effects of furosemide may be diminished. Patients should be closely monitored, and the administration of furosemide and sucralfate should be separated by at least two hours. Sucralfate may increase the absorption of aluminum when taken with vitamin D analogs, potentially leading to toxicity. Co-administration should be avoided, especially in patients with chronic renal failure or those undergoing dialysis. Magnesium sulfate/potassium chloride and sodium sulfate/potassium sulfate/magnesium sulfate can increase the toxicity of sucralfate by causing fluid and electrolyte abnormalities, which may raise the risk of seizures, arrhythmias, and renal impairment. Caution and close monitoring are advised when these combinations are used. Sucralfate is minimally absorbed and acts locally at the site of ulcers. It does not alter the recurrence or severity of duodenal ulceration after healing. However, it may interfere with the absorption of other drugs. To avoid interactions, other medications should be taken at least two hours before sucralfate. Patients with chronic renal failure or those undergoing dialysis should use sucralfate with caution due to the risk of increased aluminum absorption. Additionally, sucralfate tablets should be used cautiously in patients with swallowing difficulties or altered gag or cough reflexes. Adverse effects of sucralfate include constipation (2%), diarrhea, dizziness, dry mouth, flatulence, headache, indigestion, insomnia, nausea, vertigo, vomiting, gastrointestinal discomfort, hypersensitivity reactions, hyperglycemia (especially in diabetic patients), and bezoar formation. Fatal complications, such as pulmonary and cerebral emboli, have been reported with inappropriate intravenous administration of the oral suspension. Sucralfate oral suspension should only be administered via the oral route. Sucralfate is classified as pregnancy category B, indicating that controlled studies in pregnant women show no evidence of fetal risk. It is likely safe during lactation, as it is minimally absorbed and it is unknown whether it is excreted in breast milk. The onset of action for sucralfate is 1 to 2 hours, with a duration of up to 6 hours. It is not metabolized and is primarily excreted unchanged in the urine. It is dialyzable.
